title: Lecture 2: Chinese Economy and Financial Sectors

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hey, welcome back. Maya here.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And Leo. And today is the history episode, which, I'm gonna say it, is my favorite lecture so far.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Same, honestly. Lecture two is called Chinese Economy and Financial Sectors. And the big question on the slide is, since nineteen forty nine, how did China's economy and financial system evolve, and why this way?

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: The "why this way" part is what makes it interesting.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Totally. Because the professor's final line is something like, China's financial system is not a delayed copy of the West. It's the answer to a specific growth model.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, let's start with where China is today. Give me the headline numbers.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So, in twenty twenty four. GDP around eighteen point eight trillion dollars, second in the world. Trade around six point one trillion, first in the world. Foreign exchange reserves around three point two trillion, also first.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Second, first, first.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's exactly how the slide puts it. But then, the catch. GDP per person is only about thirteen thousand four hundred dollars. Roughly seventieth in the world.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Huge economy, but still a middle income country per person.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. And the structure changed completely. In nineteen fifty two, agriculture was fifty one percent of the economy. In twenty twenty four, it's seven percent. Services went from twenty eight percent to fifty five.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Agrarian society, world factory, service economy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. And the slide makes a point that's easy to miss. That shift itself was growth. When a farmer moves to a factory, they become way more productive, even if nothing else changes.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the growth numbers are kind of absurd.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: GDP went from about sixty billion dollars in nineteen sixty to eighteen point eight trillion. That's about three hundred and fifteen times.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay but, there's an asterisk there, right?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Good catch. That's nominal dollars, so it includes inflation and the currency getting stronger. In real terms it's more like a hundred to a hundred and twenty times. Still insane. Around ten percent a year for forty years, and over eight hundred million people out of extreme poverty.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And now it's slowing down to about five.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right, which matters for everything later.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, so rewind. Nineteen forty nine. What did China look like?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Really, really poor. GDP per person around fifty or sixty dollars. Eighty five to ninety percent of people rural. Life expectancy thirty five to forty. Literacy maybe twenty to thirty percent. And steel production, just to give you a sense, about a hundred and fifty eight thousand tons.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And today?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: About one billion tons.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Wow.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah. So, why a planned economy? The country just came out of a civil war, it's mostly farmers, almost no industry. The leadership chose a model with three pieces. The state allocates resources, agriculture gets collectivized, and heavy industry comes first.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that leads to rationing, shortage economy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. And then three phases. Reconstruction and the first five year plan, which actually built heavy industry. Then the Great Leap Forward and the Great Famine, which was massive misallocation. And then the Cultural Revolution, which was stagnation.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So by nineteen seventy eight, things were not good.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The slides give four reasons reform became unavoidable. One, growth was really low. GDP per person was a hundred and fifty six dollars.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Compare that to, what, the US?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ten thousand five hundred. Japan eight thousand eight hundred. South Korea fourteen hundred. Even India was at two hundred and six. So China was below India.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That's the wake up call.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Two, agriculture couldn't feed seven hundred and ninety million people. About a tenth of a hectare of land per person. Three, industry was inefficient. State owned firms made about seventy eight percent of output, but they had what's called a soft budget constraint.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Explain that one, because it comes back a lot.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: A soft budget constraint means if a firm loses money, someone, usually the state or a state bank, just bails it out. So there's no real pressure to be efficient. Losses don't kill you.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which, yeah, kills incentives.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And four, a big technology gap. R and D under one percent of GDP.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. So, nineteen seventy eight. What actually changed?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The approach first. Two famous phrases. It doesn't matter if the cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And crossing the river by feeling for the stones.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Basically, be pragmatic, experiment, pilot things, go step by step. And then four pillars of reform.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Rural reform first.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rural first, because the crisis was deepest there. And there's this great story. Xiaogang village. In nineteen seventy eight, eighteen families secretly signed an agreement to divide the collective land and farm it household by household.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Secretly, because it was technically illegal.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, it was risky. And their output jumped massively that year. That became the household responsibility system. Nationally, grain output went from about three hundred million tons to four hundred million by nineteen eighty four, and farm incomes doubled in six years.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that freed up labor for the township enterprises.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. The slide calls it the first pot of gold of China's reform. And it gave the reformers legitimacy for everything after.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Then SOE reform, state owned enterprises. And that took, what, thirty years?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Thirty plus. And the lecture's point is that each step fixed the previous step's problems but created new ones. First decentralization, letting managers keep some profit. Then tax for profit and contracting. Then in the nineties, the modern enterprise system, and a slogan, grasp the big, release the small.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Keep the big important firms, let go of the small ones.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. That's the Zhu Rongji era, with huge layoffs. Then in two thousand three, SASAC is created to manage state assets, and firms list on the stock market. And since twenty thirteen, mixed ownership.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Third pillar, prices. This one's my favorite. Dual track pricing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's so clever, and also kind of messy. So, instead of freeing all prices at once, which could cause a massive shock, China ran two prices at the same time. Goods inside the plan quota were sold at the low plan price. Anything produced above the quota could be sold at the market price.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So firms learn what market prices are, without blowing up the system.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Prices get discovered gradually. But, the downside. If you can buy steel at the plan price and sell it at the market price...

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Free money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Free money. Rent seeking, what they called official speculation. And in nineteen eighty eight there was an attempt at a big price breakthrough, liberalizing everything at once, and it caused panic buying and inflation. It was mostly unified after nineteen ninety two.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So gradual change isn't free.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's literally the lesson on the slide. Transitional institutions create new vested interests.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the fourth pillar is opening up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From the edges inward. Nineteen eighty, the first special economic zones, Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, and Xiamen. Nineteen eighty four, fourteen coastal cities. Nineteen ninety, Pudong in Shanghai. And then the big one, joining the WTO in two thousand one.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the phrase there is reform through opening.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. Opening wasn't just about foreign money and technology. Joining global rules forced China to change domestic institutions. The WTO was a watershed. Trade soared, manufacturing upgraded, and financial reform sped up.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, so reform is one engine. What else drove growth?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The slides add four more. People, savings, exports, and urbanization. First the demographic dividend. Working age population went from four hundred million in nineteen eighty to nine hundred million in twenty ten.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that's reversing now.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right, it peaked around twenty ten. Second, a very high savings rate. National savings above forty percent of GDP, the highest of any major economy.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Why so high?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Partly precautionary. Weak social security, so families save for health, education, housing, retirement. And partly corporate savings, firms keeping profits. And here's the link to finance. Savings go into bank deposits, banks lend them out for investment. Savings, bank loans, investment. That's the cash loop of a bank led system.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Then exports, after the WTO.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: About twenty percent growth a year. Thirty percent of world manufacturing. That trade surplus is where the three point two trillion in reserves came from. And then urbanization, from eighteen percent in nineteen seventy eight to sixty seven percent today, plus massive infrastructure. Forty five thousand kilometers of high speed rail.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which was great, but also built up local government debt.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Every engine has a cost. Okay, and now, honestly, the most important slide in the lecture. The fifty six seven eight nine.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Ah, yes. Explain it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So private firms in China account for more than fifty percent of tax revenue, more than sixty percent of GDP, more than seventy percent of innovation, more than eighty percent of urban jobs, and more than ninety percent of all firms.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Five, six, seven, eight, nine.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. But. Credit is allocated mostly by state owned banks, which historically prefer lending to state firms. So the slide says, output is produced privately, credit is allocated through a state owned system.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And every later lecture is about bridging that gap.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Every one. Banks, bonds, shadow banking, peer to peer lending. They're all attempts to get money to the private sector. And every failure in the course is a failure to bridge that gap.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: That's a great framing. Okay, finance. Before nineteen seventy eight, was there even a financial system?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not really. The lecture says banks were cashiers of the state. The People's Bank was everything at once. Central bank, commercial bank, cashier. Investment came from fiscal grants that didn't need to be repaid. No bond market, no stock market, no insurance.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So money didn't really allocate anything.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It was just an accounting tool. Which is why financial reform had to start from scratch.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then six stages.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Quickly. Nineteen seventy nine to eighty four, restoration. Four specialized state banks come back, and grants become loans. Eighty five to ninety three, marketization. The central bank separates, stock exchanges are born, and there are two big inflations. Ninety four to two thousand one, legal reform. Laws for the central bank and commercial banks, and bad loans get stripped out of the banks.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Into those asset management companies from lecture one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. Then two thousand two to twenty fifteen, post WTO expansion. Banks list on stock exchanges, there's the four trillion yuan stimulus in two thousand eight, and shadow banking explodes. And since twenty seventeen, risk control. New asset management rules, deleveraging, and fintech oversight.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the thread through all of it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Crisis forces reform. Financial reform in China is problem driven, not design driven.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. And today's system is described as bank led.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Indirect finance is about two thirds. The big six state banks hold about half of all banking assets. Credit is steered by policy. Plus capital controls, a managed exchange rate. And the lecture insists these aren't flaws. They're rational choices for a certain stage. The real question is when they work and when they turn into risk.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which brings us to the costs.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Four of them. Inequality, the Gini went from point three one to a peak of point four nine. Pollution. And the two financial ones the course focuses on. Corporate debt, around a hundred and sixty percent of GDP, plus hidden local government debt, estimated at sixty to seventy trillion yuan. And financial fragility, shadow banking, property loans, weak smaller banks.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then the last part is like, the theory part. Why does the Chinese government make decisions this way?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three components. One, pilot first. Try it in a special zone or a pilot city. If it works, scale it up. If not, the damage stays small. The slide links this to Hayek's knowledge problem. No central planner can know everything, so you let experiments generate the information.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Two, fiscal decentralization.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Local governments get to keep revenue and officials get promoted based on GDP growth. It's like a tournament. That's from Blanchard and Shleifer, two thousand one. Great for growth, but it also creates duplicate projects and local debt.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And three, dual track transition.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Protect the existing stock, liberalize the increment. Like the dual pricing. It reduces resistance, but creates rents.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So if someone asks you on the exam, what's the logic of Chinese financial decision making?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Information, political feasibility, and cost allocation. Who knows what's working, can the reform survive the people who'd lose from it, and who pays. And who pays decides the next round of reform.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Love it. Okay, three things to remember?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One. China went from a hundred and fifty six dollars per person in nineteen seventy eight to the second largest economy, through gradual, pilot based reform. Rural first, then SOEs, prices, and opening up. Two. The fifty six seven eight nine. Private firms produce the output, but state banks allocate the credit. And three. The financial system was built step by step, each step forced by a crisis. It's problem driven, not design driven.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Next time, the central bank. Lots of acronyms.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So many acronyms. See you then.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Bye.
